sources.claim: Wikipedia overview of LGBTQ rights in Brazil: the national legal timeline - recognition of same-sex unions and marriage (STF 2011/CNJ 2013), adoption, discrimination protections, gender identity and expression (the March 2018 rulings allowing name/gender-marker change without surgery), conversion therapy, military service and blood donation, plus a section listing non-binary marker rules by federative unit. Framework is national; state-level variation is not covered by this page.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2012 -> March 2026 file): same-sex relations legal throughout the country; legal gender recognition possible by self-determination; a 2019 Supreme Court ruling prohibits discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds; marriage equality since 2013 with active repeal efforts in Congress; Brazil continues to have one of the highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people; 3,000+ openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections; a 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling allows nonbinary civil-registry amendments; executive pro-rights vs a conservative legislature generating a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals.

Brazilian law-firm guide to LGBTQ+ legal rights for expats (updated April 2026): protections were established by the judiciary (STF/CNJ) rather than statute - same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality, joint adoption, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and criminalisation of homophobia/transphobia as equivalent to racism; major cities broadly welcoming with legal infrastructure accustomed to same-sex marriages and name changes; the guide states smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction, 'though the legal rights are identical nationwide'.

records.name: Puducherry
records.current_summary: No Puducherry-specific trans-related law, enforcement series or incident pattern is documented. As a union territory with a partial legislature, state-level protective policy here depends on the Union government - RTI research into India's transgender welfare boards notes that union-territory structure among the drivers of the welfare-board gap.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch dispatch (26 March 2026) on the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill passed by Parliament: it removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, limits legal recognition to historically recognised socio-cultural groups (hijra, kinnar) and intersex people, drops recognition for self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people, mandates medical certification for identity documents, and in HRW's assessment increases the risk of wrongful prosecution; protests followed the vote in Mumbai and elsewhere.

BBC report (26 March 2026): Parliament passed the amendment bill changing how transgender people are legally defined and recognised; the government says it makes welfare benefits more accessible and strengthens the 2019 law against exploitation and trafficking, while critics warn it would exclude many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people from legal recognition; notes roughly two million transgender people in India and the bill awaiting presidential assent; cited as the current national framework shift bearing on every state and union territory.

Times of India (18 August 2024, Kolkata): a group of trans women travelling to a medical college reported that a railway protection force constable groped one of them at a metro station while 'checking her gender', with an FIR filed and intrusive questioning reported; cited in the country dossier as an example of the document-and-body 'gender check' harassment trans people face at transport hubs - a West Bengal incident with no direct bearing on Puducherry.

flags: Clause 'RTI research into India's transgender welfare boards notes that union-territory structure among the drivers of the welfare-board gap' — the Quint RTI investigation is NOT among this packet's audited sources, and where it exists (other packets) it reports '19 states and UTs still don't have a welfare body' without attributing the gap to UT structure specifically.

Verfassungsblog constitutional-law essay (Clara Wellhäußer, 18 March 2026, 'Selbstbestimmung hinter Gittern') on how the Länder are rewriting prison-execution codes for trans inmates: a majority of the 16 states - the essay names Rhineland-Palatinate (new § 17 LJVollzG in force 1 March 2026), Bavaria, Saxony and Hamburg - have replaced placement rules unchanged since the 1970s, all anchoring placement to the civil-registry sex entry, which the author argues is constitutionally avoidable (self-declaration would suffice) and partly doubtful. A resident-detention analysis applying nationwide, not a visitor-facing per-Land deviation.
